title: "Part 4 — Files you will meet"

Most files that you work with are **plain text**: files that a person can read
and any program can process. This part covers the formats that you will meet in
every subject.

::: {.callout-note}
## This page grows

These are the formats that you will meet first. We add other formats when they
become useful. The page does not need to be complete to be useful.
:::

# Plain text, and what "plain" means

A plain text file contains characters and nothing else: no fonts, no colours,
no hidden formatting. This is why it lasts. A text file from thirty years ago
still opens today, and every programming language can read it without an extra
library.

A `.docx` or `.xlsx` file is **not** plain text. It is a zip archive full of
markup. This is why a program that expects text fails on it.

```bash
printf "just some text\n" > plain.txt
cat plain.txt
```

```text
just some text
```

The file extension is a hint for *you*. It does not define the file.
`data.csv`, `data.txt` and `data` can contain exactly the same bytes. If you
rename a file, you do not convert it.

# Markdown

**Markdown** (`.md`) is text with a few simple formatting marks that are still
easy to read as text. READMEs, documentation and notes are written in Markdown,
and GitHub shows it formatted on the main page of a repository.

```bash
cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# My project

A short description of what this does.

## Requirements

- Something you need
- Something else

Run it with `pixi run analysis`, and see [the notes](notes.md) for detail.

**Important:** the data is not in this repository.
EOF
head -n 3 README.md
```

```text
# My project

A short description of what this does.
```

This is all the syntax you need at the start:

| you write | you get |
|---|---|
| `# Title`, `## Section` | headings, one `#` per level |
| `*text*` or `_text_` | *italic* |
| `**text**` | **bold** |
| `` `code` `` | `inline code` |
| `- item` | a bullet list |
| `1. item` | a numbered list |
| `[label](target)` | a link |
| `> quoted` | a quotation |

Code with several lines goes in a block between three backticks. Name the
language, so that the code is highlighted:

````text
```python
print("hello")
```
````

::: {.callout-tip}
## Every repository should have a README.md

It is the first thing that anyone sees, including you in a year. It needs four
things: what the project is, what you need to run it, how to run it, and where
the data is. That is enough. A short README that exists is better than a long
one that does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Markdown is not one standard

Different tools support slightly different extensions. Tables, footnotes,
task lists and strikethrough are common, but not every tool supports them. You
will meet GitHub's version most often. If something looks right on GitHub but
not in another tool, this is usually the reason, and it is not your mistake.
:::

# JSON

Programs use **JSON** (`.json`) to pass structured data to each other. Many
tools write a JSON report in addition to their output for people. It is usually
the easiest file to get numbers from.

```bash
cat > report.json <<'EOF'
{
  "sample": "A1",
  "passed": true,
  "count": 1420,
  "score": 0.97,
  "flags": ["short", "duplicated"],
  "source": {
    "instrument": "bench-2",
    "operator": null
  }
}
EOF
cat report.json
```

JSON has six data types, and that is the whole language:

| | |
|---|---|
| **string** | `"A1"` — always double quotes, never single |
| **number** | `1420`, `0.97` — no quotes |
| **boolean** | `true` / `false` — lowercase |
| **null** | `null` — a value that is missing on purpose |
| **array** | `[...]` — an ordered list |
| **object** | `{...}` — named fields, like the whole file |

An object can contain other objects. This is how JSON shows structure: `source`
above is an object inside an object.

## Reading it

Python reads JSON without any extra installation:

```bash
python3 -c "
import json
d = json.load(open('report.json'))
print(d['sample'], d['count'])
print(d['source']['instrument'])
print(len(d['flags']), 'flags')
"
```

```text
A1 1420
bench-2
2 flags
```

Note how you read nested values: `d['source']['instrument']` goes down one
level at a time, in the same structure as the file.

## Checking whether a file is valid

A JSON file is either valid or not, and one missing comma makes the whole file
invalid. Instead of searching for the error by eye, run:

```bash
python3 -m json.tool report.json > /dev/null && echo "valid JSON"
```

```text
valid JSON
```

This command also formats the file for reading. So it is the quickest way to
make a long single-line file readable:

```bash
printf '{"a":1,"b":[2,3]}' > tight.json
python3 -m json.tool tight.json
```

```text
{
    "a": 1,
    "b": [
        2,
        3
    ]
}
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The three things that break JSON

- **A comma after the last item.** `[1, 2, 3,]` is invalid. Most programming
  languages allow it, but JSON does not.
- **Single quotes.** `{'a': 1}` is not JSON, it is Python. JSON needs `"a"`.
- **Comments.** JSON has no comments. A line with `#` or `//` makes the file
  invalid.

All three cause an error message with a line number. This line number is often
*after* the real mistake, because the program stops reading only there.
:::

# Tables: CSV and TSV

Tables usually come as one row per line, with the columns separated by a
character: a comma (**CSV**) or a tab (**TSV**).

```bash
cat > samples.csv <<'EOF'
id,group,value
A1,control,0.42
A2,control,0.51
B1,treated,0.88
EOF
column -s, -t samples.csv
```

```text
id  group    value
A1  control  0.42
A2  control  0.51
B1  treated  0.88
```

The tools from Part 1 work directly on these files:

```bash
wc -l samples.csv
head -n 1 samples.csv
grep "treated" samples.csv
```

```text
4 samples.csv
id,group,value
B1,treated,0.88
```

`cut` selects columns:

```bash
cut -d, -f2 samples.csv | sort | uniq -c
```

```text
      1 group
      2 control
      1 treated
```

`-d,` sets the separator, and `-f2` selects field 2. Note that the header was
counted too. These tools see lines, not tables, and they do not know what a
header is.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Prefer TSV when you get the choice

Real data contains commas: in names, in descriptions, in any free text. CSV
puts such a field in quotes. Then `cut -d,` gives a wrong result, because `cut`
does not understand quotes.

Tabs almost never appear inside a value. So TSV avoids the problem
completely.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Never open data in Excel "only to look at it"

Excel changes data without telling you, and when you save, the changes become
permanent:

- text that looks like a date becomes a date, and you cannot undo it
- zeros at the start are removed, so `007` becomes `7`
- long identifiers become scientific notation
- the separator and the encoding can change when you save

This problem is well documented, and it happens again and again in real
published datasets. Use `head`, `less` or VS Code instead.
:::

# Two things that break text files

You cannot see either of them on the screen. This is why you should know
them.

## Line endings

Windows ends a line with two characters (`\r\n`). Linux and macOS use one
(`\n`). So a file written on Windows and read on Linux can have an extra `\r`
at the end of every line. You cannot see it, but it makes `"control"` and
`"control\r"` different strings, and comparisons fail without an error
message.

```bash
printf 'value\r\n' > windows.txt
cat -e windows.txt
```

```text
value^M$
```

`cat -e` makes it visible: `^M` is the carriage return, and `$` is the end of
the line. To fix it:

```bash
tr -d '\r' < windows.txt > fixed.txt
cat -e fixed.txt
```

```text
value$
```

::: {.callout-tip}
VS Code shows `LF` or `CRLF` in its status bar, and a click on it converts the
file. So open a strange file in VS Code first.
:::

## Encoding

Text is stored as bytes, and an **encoding** defines which bytes mean which
characters. Today, **UTF-8** is used everywhere, and it covers every language
and symbol.

You meet this problem when a name with an umlaut or an accent appears as `Ã¼`
or `?`. The file was written in one encoding and read in another. Save the file
as UTF-8, and the problem disappears.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The safest habit

Use only plain ASCII in **file names, column headers and identifiers**:
letters, digits, underscores and hyphens. Umlauts, spaces and accents in a file
name are allowed, but sooner or later they break a tool that was not tested
with them.

Inside the *content* of a document, use any characters you like. The names are
what programs pass to each other.
:::
